notes.front: What is Google Threat Intelligence?
notes.back: A Google service that supplies curated information on attackers, signs of compromise and known attack techniques.
notes.explanation: It pools what several sources see about threats, so an organisation can act on threats before they reach it.
notes.example: Like a weather service for cyber attacks: it warns which storms are heading your way, not only that it is raining.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Trust and Security with Google Cloud”, p. 12
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is Mandiant, in the context of Google Threat Intelligence?
notes.back: Google's threat intelligence experts, whose frontline incident-response experience is one source of Google Threat Intelligence.
notes.explanation: Its analysts can also work with a customer's own team, for example through training or help from an expert inside the console.
notes.example: Like a detective agency that has worked the crime scenes itself and shares what it learnt with your guards.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Threat Intelligence - know who's targeting you”, “Make Google part of your security team”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is VirusTotal, in the context of Google Threat Intelligence?
notes.back: A crowdsourced threat-detection source feeding Google Threat Intelligence.
notes.explanation: The exam guide names it beside Google's own visibility and Mandiant's expertise; its strength is that its detections come from the crowd.
notes.example: Like a neighbourhood watch in which many members report suspicious visitors to one shared noticeboard.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader exam guide, “Section 5.2”, p. 5
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is Security Command Center (SCC)?
notes.back: Google Cloud's cloud-based risk management solution for preventing, detecting and responding to security issues.
notes.explanation: It is aimed at security professionals and helps keep the cloud environment secure.
notes.example: Like a building's security control room, with the feeds from every camera and alarm on one wall.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Security Command Center overview”
notes.evidence: Security Command Center is a cloud-based risk management solution that helps security professionals to prevent, detect, and respond to security issues. It helps to keep your cloud environment secure

notes.front: What is Google Security Operations?
notes.back: A cloud service in which enterprises privately keep, analyse and search the large volumes of security and network telemetry they generate.
notes.explanation: It normalises, indexes and correlates that data to give instant analysis and context on risky activity.
notes.example: Like a central archive and reading room where every alarm log from every branch is filed, indexed and cross-referenced.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Google SecOps overview”, “Google SecOps overview”
notes.evidence: Google Security Operations is a cloud service, built as a specialized layer on top of Google infrastructure, designed for enterprises to privately retain, analyze, and search the large amounts of security and network telemetry they generate. Google SecOps normalizes, indexes, correlates, and analyzes the data to provide instant analysis and context on risky activity.

notes.front: What is Google SecOps?
notes.back: The short name for Google Security Operations.
notes.explanation: Google's documentation titles its overview page with both names for the same service.
notes.example: Like calling Cloud Storage simply "storage" once everyone knows which service you mean.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Google SecOps overview”
notes.evidence: Google SecOps overview | Google Security Operations

notes.front: What is Gemini in Google SecOps?
notes.back: A generative AI feature built into the Google SecOps platform that works like a virtual security analyst.
notes.explanation: Its purpose is to speed up the detection, investigation and response work that security analysts do.
notes.example: Like giving a stretched night-shift analyst a tireless assistant who reads every alert and drafts the next step.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Trust and Security with Google Cloud”, p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is AI Protection?
notes.back: A Security Command Center capability for managing the security posture of AI workloads and detecting threats and risks to them.
notes.explanation: It gives a view of AI security across your Google Cloud environment, including your inventory of AI assets.
notes.example: Like an inventory-and-alarm system kept only for the models and agents a company runs.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “AI Protection overview”
notes.evidence: AI Protection helps you manage the security posture of your AI workloads by providing a view of AI security across your Google Cloud environment, and helping you to detect threats and mitigate risks to your AI inventory.

notes.front: What is Model Armor?
notes.back: A Google Cloud service that screens the prompts sent to, and responses from, large language models in AI applications.
notes.explanation: By screening both directions it protects against various risks and supports responsible AI practices.
notes.example: Like a mail room that opens and checks letters going into and out of the building.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Model Armor overview”
notes.evidence: Model Armor is a Google Cloud service designed to enhance the security and safety of your AI applications. It works by proactively screening LLM prompts and responses, protecting against various risks and ensuring responsible AI practices.

notes.front: What is a Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) network?
notes.back: A virtual version of a physical network, implemented inside Google's production network.
notes.explanation: Among other things, it provides the network connectivity for your Compute Engine virtual machines.
notes.example: Like your own private office floor, with its own corridors and doors, inside a tower the landlord runs.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “VPC networks”, “VPC networks”
notes.evidence: A Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) network is a virtual version of a physical network that is implemented inside of Google's production network by using Andromeda. A VPC network does the following: - Provides connectivity for your Compute Engine virtual machine (VM) instances.

notes.front: What is Cloud VPN?
notes.back: A service that securely extends your own network to a VPC network through an encrypted IPsec connection.
notes.explanation: One gateway encrypts the traffic and the other decrypts it, which protects the data while it travels between the networks.
notes.example: Like an armoured van carrying your parcels between your office and your cloud floor along public roads.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud VPN overview”
notes.evidence: Cloud VPN securely extends your peer network to your Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) network through an IPsec VPN connection. The VPN connection encrypts traffic traveling between the networks, with one VPN gateway handling encryption and the other handling decryption. This process protects your data during transmission.

notes.front: What is HA VPN?
notes.back: The high-availability type of Cloud VPN, offering 99.99% or 99.9% service availability depending on topology and configuration.
notes.explanation: Like Cloud VPN in general, it connects an on-premises network to a VPC network through an IPsec connection.
notes.example: Like running two armoured vans instead of one, so a single breakdown does not stop deliveries.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud VPN overview”, “HA VPN”
notes.evidence: HA VPN is a high-availability (HA) Cloud VPN solution that lets you securely connect your on-premises network to your VPC network through an IPsec VPN connection. Based on the topology and configuration, HA VPN can provide an SLA of 99.99% or 99.9% service availability.

notes.front: What is Cloud Interconnect?
notes.back: A service providing low-latency, high-availability connections for reliably transferring data between your networks and Google's.
notes.explanation: It offers several options for extending your network.
notes.example: Like a private rail siding running from your warehouse straight into the cloud depot.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Interconnect overview”
notes.evidence: Cloud Interconnect provides low-latency, high-availability connections that enable you to reliably transfer data between your networks. Cloud Interconnect offers the following options for extending your network:

notes.front: What are VPC firewall rules?
notes.back: Rules that allow or deny connections to or from the virtual machines in a VPC network.
notes.explanation: Enabled rules are always enforced, whatever the instance's configuration or operating system, even before it has started up.
notes.example: Like the guard list at each office door, saying who may come in and who may go out.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “VPC firewall rules”
notes.evidence: VPC firewall rules let you allow or deny connections to or from virtual machine (VM) instances in your VPC network. Enabled VPC firewall rules are always enforced, protecting your instances regardless of their configuration and operating system, even if they have not started up.

notes.front: What is Cloud Armor?
notes.back: A Google Cloud service that helps protect deployments from distributed denial-of-service attacks and web application attacks.
notes.explanation: It covers floods of traffic as well as application attacks such as cross-site scripting.
notes.example: Like door staff at a venue who turn away both crushing crowds and known troublemakers before they reach the bar.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Armor overview”
notes.evidence: Google Cloud Armor helps protect your Google Cloud deployments from threats such as distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks and application attacks like cross-site scripting (XSS) and SQL injection (SQLi).

notes.front: What is Identity and Access Management (IAM) in Google Cloud?
notes.back: Google Cloud's tool for fine-grained authorisation: controlling who can do what on which resources.
notes.explanation: The phrase "who can do what on which resources" is the whole job: an identity, an action and a target.
notes.example: Like a hotel key-card system deciding which guest's card opens which doors.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “IAM overview”
notes.evidence: IAM is a tool to manage fine-grained authorization for Google Cloud. In other words, it lets you control who can do what on which resources.

notes.front: In IAM, what is a principal?
notes.back: One or more identities that have authenticated to Google Cloud, and to which access can be given.
notes.explanation: Older material calls principals "members".
notes.example: Like the named guest on a hotel booking, which may be one person or a whole party.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “IAM overview”, “Principals”
notes.evidence: In Google Cloud you control access for principals. Principals represent one or more identities that have authenticated to Google Cloud. In the past, principals were referred to as members.

notes.front: What is an IAM role?
notes.back: A collection of permissions; granting the role to a principal gives it all of those permissions.
notes.explanation: You cannot grant permissions to a principal directly, only through roles.
notes.example: Like a job title that comes with a fixed bundle of building keys.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “IAM overview”, “Permissions and roles”
notes.evidence: You can't directly grant permissions to a principal. Instead, you give principals permissions by granting them roles. Roles are collections of permissions. When you grant a role to a principal, you give that principal all of the permissions in that role.

notes.front: What is an allow policy in IAM?
notes.back: An object attached to a Google Cloud resource that grants roles to principals.
notes.explanation: Older material calls allow policies "IAM policies".
notes.example: Like the access list pinned to one door, naming who holds which key to it.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “IAM overview”, “Allow policies”
notes.evidence: You grant roles to principals using allow policies. In the past, these policies were referred to as IAM policies. An allow policy is a YAML or JSON object that's attached to a Google Cloud resource.

notes.front: What are Cloud Audit Logs?
notes.back: Audit logs, written by Google Cloud services, that record administrative activities and access to resources.
notes.explanation: They let you answer "who did what, where, and when?" within your Google Cloud resources.
notes.example: Like a secure building's visitors' book combined with its door-entry log.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Audit Logs overview”
notes.evidence: Google Cloud services write audit logs that record administrative activities and resource access. You can use Cloud Audit Logs to answer "who did what, where, and when?" within your Google Cloud resources

notes.front: What is Sensitive Data Protection?
notes.back: A service that discovers, classifies and de-identifies sensitive data, inside and outside Google Cloud.
notes.explanation: It covers the whole job: finding sensitive data, labelling what kind it is, and removing what identifies people.
notes.example: Like a scanner that finds card numbers buried in old files and then blacks them out.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Sensitive Data Protection overview”
notes.evidence: Sensitive Data Protection helps you discover, classify, and de-identify sensitive data inside and outside Google Cloud.

notes.front: What is Confidential Computing?
notes.back: Protection of data while it is in use, by means of a hardware-based Trusted Execution Environment.
notes.explanation: Those environments are secure and isolated, preventing unauthorised access to or changes of applications and data while they are in use.
notes.example: Like doing sensitive sums inside a locked booth that nobody else can open or see into.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Confidential Computing overview”
notes.evidence: Confidential Computing is the protection of data in-use using a hardware-based Trusted Execution Environment (TEE). TEEs are secure and isolated environments that prevent unauthorized access or modification of applications and data while they are in use.

notes.front: What is Certificate Manager?
notes.back: A service that simplifies getting, deploying and managing Transport Layer Security certificates.
notes.explanation: It can deploy certificates on Google Cloud load balancers, among other targets.
notes.example: Like an office that renews every branch's licences before they lapse and posts them to the right doors.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Certificate Manager overview”
notes.evidence: Certificate Manager simplifies the acquisition, deployment, and management of Transport Layer Security (TLS) certificates. Certificate Manager supports deployment of global and regional certificates on Google Cloud load balancers

notes.front: What is Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP)?
notes.back: A central authorisation layer for web applications, so access is controlled per application instead of by network-level firewalls.
notes.explanation: Its policies can be defined centrally and applied to all of an organisation's applications and resources.
notes.example: Like a receptionist checking badges at each department's door rather than relying on the fence round the site.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Identity-Aware Proxy overview”
notes.evidence: IAP lets you establish a central authorization layer for applications accessed by HTTPS, so you can use an application-level access control model instead of relying on network-level firewalls. IAP policies scale across your organization. You can define access policies centrally and apply them to all of your applications and resources.

notes.front: The exam guide says "digital sovereignty". How does the study guide define the related idea of data sovereignty?
notes.back: Data is subject to the laws and regulations of the country where it resides.
notes.explanation: The exam guide uses the wider label "digital sovereignty"; the study guide defines the data version of it.
notes.example: Like goods in a bonded warehouse, which fall under the customs rules of the country the warehouse stands in.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Trust and Security with Google Cloud”, p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is data residency?
notes.back: The physical location where data is stored or processed.
notes.explanation: It is a matter of place; which country's laws apply is the separate sovereignty question.
notes.example: Like the street address of a warehouse, whatever rules govern it.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Trust and Security with Google Cloud”, p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is Assured Workloads?
notes.back: A service for setting a sovereign data and access boundary, with residency, access and personnel controls, around sensitive workloads.
notes.explanation: It is meant for private- and public-sector organisations running sensitive workloads in the cloud.
notes.example: Like a fenced, separately guarded section of a shared warehouse with its own rules on storage and entry.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Overview of Assured Workloads”, “Overview of Assured Workloads”
notes.evidence: Assured Workloads enables organizations in the private and public sectors to configure a sovereign data and access boundary with residency, access, and personnel controls for sensitive workloads in the cloud.

notes.front: What is Access Transparency?
notes.back: Logs that record the actions Google personnel take when they access your data.
notes.explanation: Each entry gives the resource and action, the time, the reason, and details about the person who accessed it.
notes.example: Like a landlord's log of every time maintenance staff entered your flat, and why.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Overview of Access Transparency”, “Overview”
notes.evidence: Access Transparency logs record the actions that Google personnel take when accessing Customer Data. Access Transparency log entries include details such as the affected resource and action, the time of the action, the reason for the action, and information about the accessor.

notes.front: What is Compliance Reports Manager?
notes.back: A Google Cloud resource that gives customers on-demand access to compliance documents such as certificates and audit reports.
notes.explanation: The exam guide calls it "compliance resource manager"; Google Cloud's page names it Compliance Reports Manager.
notes.example: Like a landlord's online folder of safety certificates that tenants can download whenever an inspector calls.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Compliance reports manager”, “Compliance Reports Manager”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: The exam guide's examples of AI stack layers that Google Cloud secures include infrastructure, data, {{c1::models}}, platform and agents.
notes.explanation: Securing the stack means protecting each of these, not only the model at its centre.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader exam guide, “Section 5.2”, p. 5
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A firm worries that someone could tamper with the AI agents that act on its behalf. Is that inside the AI stack the exam guide says Google Cloud secures?
notes.back: Yes. Agents are one of the layers in the guide's examples.
notes.explanation: The guide's examples run from infrastructure and data through models and platform to agents.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader exam guide, “Section 5.2”, p. 5
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the exam guide, which source of Google Threat Intelligence contributes frontline incident-response expertise?
notes.back: Mandiant.
notes.explanation: The guide pairs each source with a strength, and Mandiant's is experience from responding to real incidents.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader exam guide, “Section 5.2”, p. 5
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the exam guide, which source of Google Threat Intelligence contributes crowdsourced threat detection?
notes.back: VirusTotal.
notes.explanation: Its detections come from a crowd of contributors, unlike Google's own visibility or Mandiant's investigations.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader exam guide, “Section 5.2”, p. 5
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the exam guide, what does Google itself contribute to Google Threat Intelligence?
notes.back: Its vast global visibility of threats.
notes.explanation: This sits beside Mandiant's frontline expertise and VirusTotal's crowdsourced detection as the third named source.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader exam guide, “Section 5.2”, p. 5
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A security team is swamped with alerts. It wants each one scored and enriched with context from Mandiant experts and the wider community, so it can handle the worst first. Which offering fits?
notes.back: Google Threat Intelligence.
notes.choices:
A) Cloud Armor
B) Google Threat Intelligence
C) Certificate Manager
D) Cloud Interconnect
notes.choicesExplained: A: Cloud Armor filters incoming web traffic; it does not score a team's alerts. C: Certificate Manager handles certificates. D: Cloud Interconnect is a network connection.
notes.explanation: Google Threat Intelligence gives a single score for alert prioritisation and adds curated context from Mandiant experts and community intelligence.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Threat Intelligence - know who's targeting you”, “Enrich and prioritize SIEM alerts”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How do the exam guide and the study guide differ on the sources behind Google Threat Intelligence?
notes.back: The exam guide names three (Google, Mandiant, VirusTotal); the study guide lists five data sources.
notes.explanation: The study guide's five are frontline, crowdsourced, open-source and human-curated threat intelligence, plus Google insights.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Trust and Security with Google Cloud”, p. 12
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the study guide, which Security Command Center capability discovers cloud assets, scans for misconfigurations and keeps checking compliance with industry standards?
notes.back: Posture management.
notes.explanation: It is about the environment's overall set-up, as opposed to weaknesses in individual workloads or live attacks.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Trust and Security with Google Cloud”, p. 12
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the study guide, which Security Command Center capability finds weaknesses in virtual machines, containers and web apps before they can be exploited?
notes.back: Vulnerability detection.
notes.explanation: It looks for flaws in advance, before an attacker uses them.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Trust and Security with Google Cloud”, p. 12
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the study guide, which Security Command Center capability watches system logs and runtime environments in real time for active threats such as malware?
notes.back: Threat detection.
notes.explanation: It deals with attacks already under way, such as unauthorised access or resource abuse.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Trust and Security with Google Cloud”, p. 12
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In Security Command Center, what is a finding?
notes.back: A record of a threat or other issue that a service has found in your cloud environments.
notes.explanation: Findings can come from Security Command Center's built-in services, integrated Google Cloud services or third-party services.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Security Command Center overview”
notes.evidence: Findings are records of threats or other issues that a service has found in your cloud environments. Findings are generated by the following sources: - Built-in: Security services that are part of Security Command Center. - Integrated: Google Cloud security services

notes.front: An internal review finds that some storage was accidentally left open to the public and that credentials were leaked. The security lead wants one Google Cloud service that keeps discovering problems like these so they can be fixed. Which fits?
notes.back: Security Command Center.
notes.choices:
A) Security Command Center
B) Cloud VPN
C) Certificate Manager
D) Cloud Interconnect
notes.choicesExplained: B: Cloud VPN encrypts traffic between networks; it does not look for exposed resources. C: Certificate Manager manages certificates. D: Cloud Interconnect provides private connections.
notes.explanation: Discovering and remediating misconfigurations, publicly exposed resources and leaked credentials is part of Security Command Center's vulnerability detection.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Security Command Center overview”
notes.evidence: Vulnerability detection: Discover and remediate problems such as misconfigurations, publicly exposed resources, leaked credentials, and resources with known risks.

notes.front: In Google SecOps, which capability brings data into the platform through forwarders, parsers, collectors, connectors and webhooks?
notes.back: Collection.
notes.explanation: It is the first step of handling a threat across its lifecycle: getting the data in.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Google SecOps overview”, “Google SecOps overview”
notes.evidence: Collection: Data is ingested into the platform using forwarders, parsers, OpenTelemetry collectors, connectors, and webhooks.

notes.front: In Google SecOps, which capability aggregates and normalises the data and links it to detections and threat intelligence?
notes.back: Detection.
notes.explanation: Normalising the data into one model is what lets it be matched against detections and threat intelligence.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Google SecOps overview”, “Google SecOps overview”
notes.evidence: Detection: This data is aggregated, normalized using the Unified Data Model (UDM), and linked to detections and threat intelligence.

notes.front: In Google SecOps, which capability examines threats through case management, search, collaboration and context-aware analytics?
notes.back: Investigation.
notes.explanation: It comes between detecting a threat and responding to it.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Google SecOps overview”, “Google SecOps overview”
notes.evidence: Investigation: Threats are investigated through case management, search, collaboration, and context-aware analytics.

notes.front: In Google SecOps, which capability lets analysts resolve threats quickly with automated playbooks?
notes.back: Response.
notes.explanation: Automated playbooks and case management let analysts act quickly and provide resolutions.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Google SecOps overview”, “Google SecOps overview”
notes.evidence: Response: Security analysts can respond quickly and provide resolutions using automated playbooks and case management.

notes.front: A retailer wants security telemetry from many systems gathered in one place, correlated, and searchable back over many months to check whether any device has been compromised. Which fits?
notes.back: Google Security Operations.
notes.choices:
A) Cloud Armor
B) Certificate Manager
C) Google Security Operations
D) Model Armor
notes.choicesExplained: A: Cloud Armor filters incoming web traffic; it does not store telemetry. B: Certificate Manager manages certificates. D: Model Armor screens prompts and responses of AI applications.
notes.explanation: Google SecOps keeps aggregated security information for months or longer and lets you search it by asset, domain or IP address for signs of compromise.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Google SecOps overview”, “Google SecOps overview”
notes.evidence: Google SecOps lets you examine the aggregated security information for your enterprise going back for months or longer. Use Google SecOps to search across all of the domains accessed within your enterprise. You can narrow your search to any specific asset, domain, or IP address to determine if any compromise has taken place.

notes.front: Which three parts of security work does Gemini in Google SecOps speed up, per the study guide?
notes.back: Threat detection, investigation and response.
notes.explanation: It acts as a virtual security analyst inside the platform, so these workflows move faster.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Trust and Security with Google Cloud”, p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A small security team already on Google SecOps has a backlog of alerts and wants a generative AI assistant inside the platform to speed up its investigations. Which fits?
notes.back: Gemini in Google SecOps.
notes.choices:
A) Model Armor
B) AI Protection
C) Sensitive Data Protection
D) Gemini in Google SecOps
notes.choicesExplained: A: Model Armor screens prompts and responses of AI applications; it does not help analysts. B: AI Protection secures AI workloads rather than assisting analysts. C: Sensitive Data Protection finds and de-identifies sensitive data.
notes.explanation: Gemini in Google SecOps is the generative AI feature in the platform that acts as a virtual security analyst.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Trust and Security with Google Cloud”, p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two capabilities of AI Protection?
notes.back: Any two, for example detecting over-privileged agents and managing the compliance of AI assets.
notes.explanation: Its capabilities also include assessing your AI asset inventory and detecting threats to AI systems.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “AI Protection overview”, “Capabilities of AI Protection”
notes.evidence: - Detect over-privileged agents: detect Agent Runtime agents that are granted excessive permissions. - Manage compliance: proactively verify that AI assets in your deployments adhere to relevant security standards.

notes.front: A bank runs several AI agents and models on Google Cloud. It wants an inventory of its AI assets and to be told when an agent has been granted excessive permissions. Which fits?
notes.back: AI Protection.
notes.choices:
A) AI Protection
B) Cloud VPN
C) Certificate Manager
D) Identity-Aware Proxy
notes.choicesExplained: B: Cloud VPN encrypts network traffic. C: Certificate Manager handles certificates. D: Identity-Aware Proxy controls user access to applications; it does not inventory AI assets.
notes.explanation: Assessing the AI asset inventory and detecting over-privileged agents are both AI Protection capabilities.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “AI Protection overview”, “Capabilities of AI Protection”
notes.evidence: - Assess your AI asset inventory: understand your AI systems and assets.

notes.front: Which two kinds of attack on AI systems does Model Armor help protect against, where attackers try to make the system do unintended things?
notes.back: Prompt injection and jailbreak attacks.
notes.explanation: Both are ways for malicious actors to manipulate AI systems into unintended actions.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Model Armor overview”, “Use cases”
notes.evidence: Protect against prompt injection and jailbreak attacks, preventing malicious actors from manipulating AI systems to perform unintended actions.

notes.front: Users of a customer-service chatbot keep typing "ignore your previous instructions and…" to make it reveal internal information. Which service screens these prompts?
notes.back: Model Armor.
notes.choices:
A) Cloud Armor
B) Model Armor
C) VPC firewall rules
D) Cloud Audit Logs
notes.choicesExplained: A: Cloud Armor filters web traffic such as floods and cross-site scripting, not the meaning of prompts. C: VPC firewall rules allow or deny network connections. D: Cloud Audit Logs record activity; they do not screen content.
notes.explanation: Tricking a model into ignoring its instructions is prompt injection, which Model Armor detects when it screens prompts.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Model Armor overview”, “Prompt injection and jailbreak detection”
notes.evidence: Prompt injection is a security vulnerability where attackers craft special commands within the text input (the prompt) to trick an AI model. This can make the AI ignore its usual instructions, reveal sensitive information, or perform actions it wasn't designed to do.

notes.front: How does Model Armor differ from AI Protection?
notes.back: Model Armor screens the prompts and responses of AI applications; AI Protection, integrated with Security Command Center, safeguards AI workloads and data.
notes.explanation: One works on the content passing through a model; the other on the security of the AI estate as a whole.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Trust and Security with Google Cloud”, p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two elements of Google's secure-by-design cloud platform, from the exam guide's examples?
notes.back: Any two, for example proprietary data centres and custom security hardware.
notes.explanation: The guide's other examples are core infrastructure, purpose-built servers and networking, and custom security software.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader exam guide, “Section 5.2”, p. 6
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Per the study guide, what does Google's purpose-built private fibre network mean for customer traffic?
notes.back: It carries all customer traffic, which greatly reduces exposure to the public internet.
notes.explanation: Keeping traffic on Google's own network also allows fast, secure communication around the world.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Trust and Security with Google Cloud”, p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two physical security measures Google uses at its own data centres?
notes.back: Any two, for example biometric identification and laser-based intrusion detection.
notes.explanation: Google designs and builds these data centres with multiple layers of physical security; metal detection, cameras and vehicle barriers are others.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Google infrastructure security design overview”, “Security of physical premises”
notes.evidence: We design and build our own data centers, which incorporate multiple layers of physical security. Access to these data centers is tightly controlled. We use multiple physical security layers to protect our data center floors. We use biometric identification, metal detection, cameras, vehicle barriers, and laser-based intrusion detection systems.

notes.front: What is Titan, in Google's infrastructure?
notes.back: A custom hardware security chip that Google designs and deploys on servers, devices and peripherals.
notes.explanation: It lets Google identify and authenticate legitimate Google devices at the hardware level, acting as a hardware root of trust.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Google infrastructure security design overview”, “Hardware design and provenance”
notes.evidence: We also design custom chips, including a hardware security chip (called Titan), that we deploy on servers, devices, and peripherals. These chips let us identify and authenticate legitimate Google devices at the hardware level and serve as hardware roots of trust.

notes.front: What are two layers shown in the study guide's picture of Google's multilayered security approach?
notes.back: Any two, for example data centres and identity.
notes.explanation: The picture also shows network security, secure storage, and operational and device security, stacked as layers of defence.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Trust and Security with Google Cloud”, p. 12
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A regulator asks how a company can trust that the servers running its Google Cloud workloads are genuine Google machines. Which part of Google's secure-by-design platform answers this most directly?
notes.back: Titan chips acting as hardware roots of trust.
notes.choices:
A) Titan chips acting as hardware roots of trust
B) Cloud Armor security policies
C) Model Armor filters
D) Certificate Manager
notes.choicesExplained: B: Cloud Armor filters incoming traffic; it says nothing about server hardware. C: Model Armor screens AI prompts and responses. D: Certificate Manager handles certificates for services, not server identity.
notes.explanation: Google's custom security chips identify and authenticate legitimate Google devices at the hardware level.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Google infrastructure security design overview”, “Hardware design and provenance”
notes.evidence: These chips let us identify and authenticate legitimate Google devices at the hardware level and serve as hardware roots of trust.

notes.front: Are VPC networks regional or global resources?
notes.back: Global. Their subnets are regional.
notes.explanation: A VPC network and its routes and firewall rules are not tied to any particular region or zone.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “VPC networks”, “Specifications”
notes.evidence: VPC networks, including their associated routes and firewall rules, are global resources. They are not associated with any particular region or zone. - Subnets are regional resources.

notes.front: A team needs private networking for virtual machines in three regions. Does it need one VPC network per region?
notes.back: No. One VPC network spans all regions, with a regional subnet in each.
notes.explanation: VPC networks are global resources, while their subnets are regional.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “VPC networks”, “Specifications”
notes.evidence: VPC networks, including their associated routes and firewall rules, are global resources. They are not associated with any particular region or zone. - Subnets are regional resources.

notes.front: Can Cloud VPN be used to route traffic to the public internet?
notes.back: No. It is designed for secure communication between private networks.
notes.explanation: It connects a peer network to a VPC network, or two VPC networks to each other.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud VPN overview”
notes.evidence: You can also connect two VPC networks together by connecting two Cloud VPN instances. You cannot use Cloud VPN to route traffic to the public internet; it is designed for secure communication between private networks.

notes.front: What service availability does a Classic VPN gateway provide, and how many interfaces does it have?
notes.back: 99.9% availability, with a single interface and a single external IP address.
notes.explanation: HA VPN, by contrast, can reach 99.99% depending on topology and configuration.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud VPN overview”, “Classic VPN”
notes.evidence: In contrast to HA VPN, Classic VPN gateways have a single interface, a single external IP address, and support tunnels that use static routing (policy based or route based). Classic VPN gateways provide an SLA of 99.9% service availability.

notes.front: A small firm wants an encrypted link from its office network to its VPC network, set up quickly over its existing internet connection and without a dedicated circuit. Which fits?
notes.back: Cloud VPN.
notes.choices:
A) Dedicated Interconnect
B) Cloud VPN
C) Identity-Aware Proxy
D) Cloud Armor
notes.choicesExplained: A: Dedicated Interconnect needs a direct physical connection to Google's network. C: Identity-Aware Proxy controls access to applications, not network-to-network links. D: Cloud Armor filters incoming web traffic.
notes.explanation: When you don't need a full Cloud Interconnect connection, Cloud VPN sets up IPsec tunnels whose encrypted traffic crosses the public internet.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Interconnect overview”, “Use Cloud VPN by itself”
notes.evidence: If you don't require an entire Cloud Interconnect connection, you can use Cloud VPN on its own to set up IPsec VPN tunnels between your VPC networks and other networks. IPsec VPN tunnels encrypt data by using industry-standard IPsec protocols. The encrypted traffic traverses the public internet.

notes.front: Does traffic over Cloud Interconnect cross the public internet?
notes.back: No. It travels over a dedicated connection, either direct or through a service provider.
notes.explanation: Bypassing the internet means fewer hops, so fewer points where traffic might be dropped or disrupted.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Interconnect overview”, “Benefits”
notes.evidence: Traffic between your networks doesn't traverse the public internet. Traffic traverses a dedicated connection or goes through a service provider with a dedicated connection. By bypassing the public internet, your traffic takes fewer hops, so there are fewer points of failure where your traffic might get dropped or disrupted.

notes.front: Does Cloud Interconnect encrypt traffic by default?
notes.back: No. You can add MACsec, or run HA VPN over Cloud Interconnect, to encrypt it.
notes.explanation: A private connection is not the same as an encrypted one, so encryption is an extra step.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Interconnect overview”, “Encrypt Cloud Interconnect traffic”
notes.evidence: Cloud Interconnect doesn't encrypt traffic by default. You can use MACsec for Cloud Interconnect to help secure traffic between your on-premises router and Google's edge routers on supported Cloud Interconnect circuits.

notes.front: How does Dedicated Interconnect differ from Partner Interconnect?
notes.back: Dedicated: a direct physical connection to Google's network. Partner: a connection through a supported service provider.
notes.explanation: Both link on-premises and VPC networks; they differ in who provides the physical link.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Interconnect overview”
notes.evidence: Provides connectivity between your on-premises and VPC networks through a direct physical connection between your on-premises network and the Google network. For more information, see the Dedicated Interconnect overview. Partner Interconnect Provides connectivity between your on-premises and VPC networks through a supported service provider.

notes.front: A bank moves very large volumes of data every night between its own data centre and Google Cloud and wants the traffic kept off the public internet. Which fits?
notes.back: Cloud Interconnect.
notes.choices:
A) Cloud VPN
B) Identity-Aware Proxy
C) Cloud Interconnect
D) Certificate Manager
notes.choicesExplained: A: Cloud VPN encrypts traffic but sends it across the public internet. B: Identity-Aware Proxy controls user access to applications. D: Certificate Manager handles certificates.
notes.explanation: Cloud Interconnect traffic travels over a dedicated connection and does not traverse the public internet.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Interconnect overview”, “Benefits”
notes.evidence: Traffic between your networks doesn't traverse the public internet. Traffic traverses a dedicated connection or goes through a service provider with a dedicated connection.

notes.front: What is the key difference between Cloud VPN and Cloud Interconnect?
notes.back: Cloud VPN runs encrypted IPsec tunnels over the public internet; Cloud Interconnect provides a full private connection instead.
notes.explanation: Cloud VPN on its own is the option when you don't need an entire Cloud Interconnect connection.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Interconnect overview”, “Use Cloud VPN by itself”
notes.evidence: If you don't require an entire Cloud Interconnect connection, you can use Cloud VPN on its own to set up IPsec VPN tunnels between your VPC networks and other networks. IPsec VPN tunnels encrypt data by using industry-standard IPsec protocols. The encrypted traffic traverses the public internet.

notes.front: VPC firewall rules are defined at the network level. At what level are connections actually allowed or denied?
notes.back: Per instance: each virtual machine's connections are allowed or denied individually.
notes.explanation: This is why every VPC network works as a distributed firewall.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “VPC firewall rules”
notes.evidence: Every VPC network functions as a distributed firewall. While firewall rules are defined at the network level, connections are allowed or denied on a per-instance basis.

notes.front: An administrator wants virtual machines in a VPC network to accept remote-login connections only from the company's office address range. Which fits?
notes.back: VPC firewall rules.
notes.choices:
A) Certificate Manager
B) Cloud Audit Logs
C) Sensitive Data Protection
D) VPC firewall rules
notes.choicesExplained: A: Certificate Manager handles certificates, not connections. B: Cloud Audit Logs record activity after the fact; they do not block it. C: Sensitive Data Protection finds and de-identifies sensitive data.
notes.explanation: A firewall rule can target traffic by protocol, destination port and source, which is exactly what this restriction needs.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “VPC firewall rules”, “Firewall rules in Google Cloud”
notes.evidence: The components enable you to target certain types of traffic, based on the traffic's protocol, destination ports, sources, and destinations.

notes.front: Where do Cloud Armor security policies permit or deny access, and what does that prevent?
notes.back: At the Google Cloud edge, close to the traffic source, so unwanted traffic never consumes resources or enters your VPC networks.
notes.explanation: Stopping traffic near its source keeps it away from the deployment it targets.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Armor overview”, “How Cloud Armor works”
notes.evidence: Cloud Armor security policies allow you to permit or deny access to your deployment at the Google Cloud edge, close to the traffic source. This prevents unwanted traffic from consuming resources or entering your Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) networks.

notes.front: What are Cloud Armor's preconfigured web application firewall rules?
notes.back: Ready-made rules containing dozens of signatures from open-source industry standards, each identifying a specific attack pattern.
notes.explanation: Google provides them as they are, so you can check traffic against many distinct signatures just by referring to named rules.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Armor overview”, “Preconfigured WAF rules”
notes.evidence: Cloud Armor preconfigured WAF rules are complex web application firewall (WAF) rules that include dozens of signatures compiled from open source industry standards. Each signature identifies a specific attack pattern within the rule set. Cloud Armor provides these rules as-is, so you can evaluate many distinct traffic signatures by referring to named rules.

notes.front: An online shop behind a global external Application Load Balancer faces floods of requests and attempts at cross-site scripting. Which service helps protect it?
notes.back: Cloud Armor.
notes.choices:
A) Model Armor
B) Cloud Interconnect
C) Sensitive Data Protection
D) Cloud Armor
notes.choicesExplained: A: Model Armor screens AI prompts and responses, not web traffic. B: Cloud Interconnect is a private network connection. C: Sensitive Data Protection finds and de-identifies sensitive data.
notes.explanation: Cloud Armor protects deployments against distributed denial-of-service attacks and application attacks such as cross-site scripting.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Armor overview”
notes.evidence: Google Cloud Armor helps protect your Google Cloud deployments from threats such as distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks and application attacks like cross-site scripting (XSS) and SQL injection (SQLi).

notes.front: What three components does giving someone permissions in IAM involve?
notes.back: A principal, a role and a resource.
notes.explanation: You grant the principal a role on the resource, using an allow policy.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “IAM overview”, “Access in Google Cloud”
notes.evidence: Giving someone permissions in IAM involves the following three components: - Principal: The identity of the person or system that you want to give permissions to. - Role: The collection of permissions that you want to give the principal. - Resource: The Google Cloud resource that you want to let the principal access.

notes.front: Which type of IAM role is managed by Google Cloud services and holds the permissions for common tasks in each service?
notes.back: Predefined roles.
notes.explanation: For example, the Pub/Sub Publisher role gives access to publish messages to a Pub/Sub topic.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “IAM overview”, “Permissions and roles”
notes.evidence: Predefined roles: Roles that are managed by Google Cloud services. These roles contain the permissions needed to perform common tasks for each given service. For example, the Pub/Sub Publisher role (roles/pubsub.publisher) provides access to publish messages to a Pub/Sub topic.

notes.front: Which type of IAM role contains only the permissions you specify, but carries a higher maintenance burden?
notes.back: Custom roles.
notes.explanation: You have complete control over their permissions, but the number of custom roles you can have is limited.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “IAM overview”, “Permissions and roles”
notes.evidence: Custom roles: Roles that you create that contain only the permissions that you specify. You have complete control over the permissions in these roles. However, they have a higher maintenance burden than predefined roles and there's a limit to the number of custom roles

notes.front: Which type of IAM role is highly permissive and should not be used in production?
notes.back: Basic roles.
notes.explanation: They give broad access to Google Cloud services, which can be useful for testing.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “IAM overview”, “Permissions and roles”
notes.evidence: Basic roles: Highly permissive roles that provide broad access to Google Cloud services. These roles can be useful for testing purposes, but shouldn't be used in production environments.

notes.front: A contractor's application only needs to publish messages to one Pub/Sub topic. Which grant best follows least privilege?
notes.back: A predefined role for publishing to Pub/Sub, granted on that topic.
notes.choices:
A) A basic role across the whole project
B) A predefined role for publishing to Pub/Sub, granted on that topic
C) The individual publish permission granted directly to the contractor
D) A custom role holding every Pub/Sub permission
notes.choicesExplained: A: basic roles are highly permissive and not for production. C: IAM does not let you grant permissions to a principal directly, only roles. D: every Pub/Sub permission is far more than publishing needs.
notes.explanation: Predefined roles hold the permissions for a common task, such as publishing messages to a Pub/Sub topic, and nothing wider.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “IAM overview”, “Permissions and roles”
notes.evidence: For example, the Pub/Sub Publisher role (roles/pubsub.publisher) provides access to publish messages to a Pub/Sub topic.

notes.front: Which type of Cloud Audit Logs records user-driven calls that change resource configuration or metadata, such as creating a virtual machine?
notes.back: Admin Activity audit logs.
notes.explanation: Changing IAM permissions is another example of what they record.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Audit Logs overview”, “Admin Activity audit logs”
notes.evidence: Admin Activity audit logs are log entries written by user-driven API calls or other actions that modify the configuration or metadata of resources. For example, these logs record when users create VM instances or change Identity and Access Management permissions.

notes.front: Which type of Cloud Audit Logs records calls that read resource configuration, or that create, modify or read user-provided data?
notes.back: Data Access audit logs.
notes.explanation: They cover reading configuration and handling the data itself, not changes to configuration.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Audit Logs overview”, “Data Access audit logs”
notes.evidence: Data Access audit logs are log entries written by API calls that read the configuration or metadata of resources. They are also written by user-driven API calls that create, modify, or read user-provided resource data.

notes.front: Which type of Cloud Audit Logs records configuration changes made by Google Cloud systems rather than by direct user action?
notes.back: System Event audit logs.
notes.explanation: For example, one is written when autoscaling adds virtual machines to, or removes them from, a managed instance group.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Audit Logs overview”, “System Event audit logs”
notes.evidence: System Event audit logs are log entries written by Google Cloud systems and managed service agents that modify the configuration of resources. System Event audit logs aren't driven by direct user action. For example, a System Event audit log is written when VMs are automatically added to or removed from managed instance groups (MIGs) due to autoscaling.

notes.front: Which type of Cloud Audit Logs is written when a Google Cloud service denies access because of a security policy violation?
notes.back: Policy Denied audit logs.
notes.explanation: They are generated by default and cannot be disabled, though exclusion filters can keep some out of storage.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Audit Logs overview”, “Policy Denied audit logs”
notes.evidence: Policy Denied audit logs are log entries written when a Google Cloud service denies access to a user or service account because of a security policy violation. Policy Denied audit logs are generated by default and your Google Cloud project is charged for log storage. You can't disable Policy Denied audit logs, but you can use exclusion filters

notes.front: Can Admin Activity audit logs be switched off?
notes.back: No. They are always written and cannot be configured, excluded or disabled.
notes.explanation: They are generated even if the logging service's interface is disabled.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Audit Logs overview”, “Admin Activity audit logs”
notes.evidence: Admin Activity audit logs are always written; you can't configure, exclude, or disable them. Even if you disable the Cloud Logging API, Admin Activity audit logs are still generated.

notes.front: An auditor asks who gave a user a new IAM role last Tuesday. Which type of Cloud Audit Logs holds the answer?
notes.back: Admin Activity audit logs.
notes.explanation: Changing IAM permissions modifies a resource's configuration, which Admin Activity audit logs record.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Audit Logs overview”, “Admin Activity audit logs”
notes.evidence: For example, these logs record when users create VM instances or change Identity and Access Management permissions.

notes.front: What does Sensitive Data Protection's discovery service produce?
notes.back: Data profiles showing where sensitive and high-risk data reside across an organisation, folder or project.
notes.explanation: Profiles hold metrics and metadata about data assets and suit scanning large amounts of data at a high level.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Sensitive Data Protection overview”, “Sensitive data discovery”
notes.evidence: The discovery service lets you generate profiles for your data across an organization, folder, or project. Data profiles contain metrics and metadata about your data assets and help you determine where sensitive and high-risk data reside.

notes.front: In Sensitive Data Protection, when do you use an inspection rather than discovery?
notes.back: When you need detailed information about each instance of sensitive data in a resource, such as one table.
notes.explanation: Discovery profiles many resources at a high level; inspection gives the exact location of every instance.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Sensitive Data Protection overview”, “Sensitive data inspection”
notes.evidence: An inspection is useful if you need detailed information about each instance of sensitive data stored in a resource, like a single BigQuery table.

notes.front: A research team wants to give analysts a patient dataset that stays useful for analysis but no longer shows who the patients are. Which fits?
notes.back: Sensitive Data Protection.
notes.choices:
A) Confidential Computing
B) Access Transparency
C) Sensitive Data Protection
D) Cloud Armor
notes.choicesExplained: A: Confidential Computing protects data while it is processed; it does not remove identifiers. B: Access Transparency logs Google personnel access. D: Cloud Armor filters web traffic.
notes.explanation: Sensitive Data Protection can transform direct and indirect identifiers so research teams can analyse data without exposing personal information.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Sensitive Data Protection overview”, “When to use Sensitive Data Protection”
notes.evidence: De-identify analytical datasets while preserving utility: Transform direct and indirect identifiers using pseudonymization, date shifting, or bucketing so research and business intelligence teams can analyze data without exposing plaintext PII.

notes.front: Of the three states of end-to-end encryption, which one does Confidential Computing provide?
notes.back: Encryption in use, protecting data while it is being processed.
notes.explanation: Encryption at rest and in transit cover stored and moving data; in use is the last piece.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Confidential Computing overview”, “End-to-end encryption”
notes.evidence: Encryption at rest protects your data while it is being stored. - Encryption in transit protects your data when it is moving between two points. - Encryption in use protects your data while it is being processed. Confidential Computing provides the last piece of end-to-end encryption: encryption in use.

notes.front: A pharmaceutical firm already encrypts its data at rest and in transit. It now wants the data protected while applications are processing it in Google Cloud. Which fits?
notes.back: Confidential Computing.
notes.choices:
A) Confidential Computing
B) Cloud VPN
C) Certificate Manager
D) Cloud Audit Logs
notes.choicesExplained: B: Cloud VPN protects data in transit between networks. C: Certificate Manager handles certificates for traffic in transit. D: Cloud Audit Logs record activity; they do not protect data.
notes.explanation: Confidential Computing adds encryption in use, the piece that at-rest and in-transit encryption leave out.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Confidential Computing overview”, “End-to-end encryption”
notes.evidence: Encryption in use protects your data while it is being processed. Confidential Computing provides the last piece of end-to-end encryption: encryption in use.

notes.front: Which two types of certificate does Certificate Manager support?
notes.back: Google-managed certificates, which Google Cloud obtains and manages, and self-managed certificates, which you obtain and renew.
notes.explanation: Google-managed certificates can be issued and renewed automatically; self-managed ones you upload and look after yourself.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Certificate Manager overview”, “Supported TLS certificates”
notes.evidence: Google-managed certificates: certificates that Google Cloud obtains and manages for you. Using Certificate Manager, you can automatically issue and renew Google-managed certificates.

notes.front: A media group serves hundreds of websites through Google Cloud load balancers and keeps missing certificate renewals. Which fits?
notes.back: Certificate Manager with Google-managed certificates.
notes.choices:
A) Cloud Armor
B) Identity-Aware Proxy
C) Sensitive Data Protection
D) Certificate Manager with Google-managed certificates
notes.choicesExplained: A: Cloud Armor filters attacks; it does not renew certificates. B: Identity-Aware Proxy controls who may reach an application. C: Sensitive Data Protection handles sensitive data.
notes.explanation: Certificate Manager can automatically issue, renew and manage Google-managed certificates, and store and deploy very many of them.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Certificate Manager overview”, “Benefits”
notes.evidence: Automatically issue, renew, and manage Google-managed certificates. - Provision Google-managed certificates in advance to enable seamless, zero-downtime migrations to Google Cloud. Security - Securely store and deploy millions of certificates.

notes.front: How can Identity-Aware Proxy limit an application to certain people?
notes.back: With group-based access, for example open to employees but not contractors, or to one department only.
notes.explanation: IAP enforces access control policies for applications and resources.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Identity-Aware Proxy overview”, “When to use IAP”
notes.evidence: With IAP, you can set up group-based application access: a resource could be accessible for employees and inaccessible for contractors, or only accessible to a specific department.

notes.front: Do users reaching an application through Identity-Aware Proxy need a VPN?
notes.back: No. They get fine-grained access controls without a VPN.
notes.explanation: IAP performs authentication and authorisation checks on every attempt to reach the secured resource.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Identity-Aware Proxy overview”, “How IAP works”
notes.evidence: When you grant a user access to an application or resource by IAP, they're subject to the fine-grained access controls implemented by the product in use without requiring a VPN. When a user tries to access an IAP-secured resource, IAP performs authentication and authorization checks.

notes.front: A firm wants staff to reach an internal web app on Cloud Run according to who they are and which team they belong to, without rolling out a VPN. Which fits?
notes.back: Identity-Aware Proxy.
notes.choices:
A) Cloud Interconnect
B) Identity-Aware Proxy
C) VPC firewall rules
D) Cloud VPN
notes.choicesExplained: A: Cloud Interconnect links networks; it does not check who a user is. C: VPC firewall rules decide by network connection, not by identity. D: Cloud VPN is the VPN the firm wants to avoid.
notes.explanation: IAP gives group-based, fine-grained access to applications without requiring a VPN.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Identity-Aware Proxy overview”, “How IAP works”
notes.evidence: When you grant a user access to an application or resource by IAP, they're subject to the fine-grained access controls implemented by the product in use without requiring a VPN.

notes.front: How does Identity-Aware Proxy's access model differ from a network-level firewall's?
notes.back: IAP controls access at the application level, from the user's identity; a network firewall controls it at the network level.
notes.explanation: IAP is meant as a central authorisation layer, used instead of relying on network-level firewalls.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Identity-Aware Proxy overview”
notes.evidence: IAP lets you establish a central authorization layer for applications accessed by HTTPS, so you can use an application-level access control model instead of relying on network-level firewalls.

notes.front: Per the study guide, what do Google's transparency reports and third-party audits shed light on?
notes.back: Government and corporate actions that affect privacy, security and access to information.
notes.explanation: They are one way Google offers customers insight into, and accountability for, how such actions are handled.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Trust and Security with Google Cloud”, p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A prospective customer's lawyers want evidence about Google Cloud's security that does not rest on Google's own word. Which of Google's trust mechanisms from the exam guide fits best?
notes.back: Third-party audits.
notes.explanation: Google Cloud's third-party audits and certifications are among the compliance resources that Compliance Reports Manager makes available on demand.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Compliance reports manager”, “Compliance Reports Manager”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Under Google Cloud's trust principles, is customer data sold to third parties or used for advertising?
notes.back: Neither. Google does not sell customer data to third parties or use it for advertising.
notes.explanation: These sit beside the principles that customers own their data and that it is encrypted by default.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Trust and Security with Google Cloud”, p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the difference between data sovereignty and data residency?
notes.back: Sovereignty is about whose laws govern the data; residency is about where it is physically stored or processed.
notes.explanation: Sovereignty follows from the country where data resides, so the two are linked but ask different questions.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Trust and Security with Google Cloud”, p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: An insurer requires that its customer records are stored only in data centres located in Germany. Is that a data residency or a data sovereignty requirement?
notes.back: Data residency: it concerns the physical location of the data.
notes.explanation: The rule names a place for storage, not which laws should apply.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Trust and Security with Google Cloud”, p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two kinds of organisation that Assured Workloads is meant for?
notes.back: Any two, for example those that must keep data in certain regions or countries, and those that must control Google personnel access.
notes.explanation: Organisations with strict rules on data storage, key management and access, such as in finance, healthcare and government, are another kind.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Overview of Assured Workloads”, “Use cases for Assured Workloads”
notes.evidence: - Organizations that must store their data within certain regions or countries. - Organizations that must control Google Cloud personnel access to their data.

notes.front: A government agency must keep its data within its own country and limit which Google personnel can reach it, while still using commercial Google Cloud. Which fits?
notes.back: Assured Workloads.
notes.choices:
A) Model Armor
B) Assured Workloads
C) Cloud Armor
D) Certificate Manager
notes.choicesExplained: A: Model Armor screens AI prompts and responses. C: Cloud Armor filters incoming web traffic. D: Certificate Manager handles certificates.
notes.explanation: Assured Workloads sets a sovereign boundary with residency, access and personnel controls while keeping the benefits of commercial cloud infrastructure.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Overview of Assured Workloads”, “Overview of Assured Workloads”
notes.evidence: Assured Workloads lets you run compliant workloads while maintaining the scale, cost, and service availability benefits of commercial cloud infrastructure.

notes.front: How do Access Transparency logs differ from Cloud Audit Logs?
notes.back: Cloud Audit Logs record actions by members of your organisation; Access Transparency logs record actions by Google personnel.
notes.explanation: Used together, they give audit logging of both customer actions and Google's administrative access.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Overview of Access Transparency”, “Overview”
notes.evidence: Cloud Audit Logs records the actions that members of your Google Cloud organization have taken in your Google Cloud resources, whereas Access Transparency logs record the actions taken by Google personnel. When used together, Cloud Audit Logs and Access Transparency logs provide you audit logging on both customer actions and Google administrative access to Customer Data.

notes.front: After raising a support case about an outage, a bank wants to verify that Google staff accessed its content only to fix that outage. Which fits?
notes.back: Access Transparency.
notes.choices:
A) Access Transparency
B) Sensitive Data Protection
C) Cloud Armor
D) Identity-Aware Proxy
notes.choicesExplained: B: Sensitive Data Protection finds and de-identifies data; it does not log Google access. C: Cloud Armor filters web traffic. D: Identity-Aware Proxy controls user access to applications.
notes.explanation: Checking that Google personnel access your content only for valid business reasons, such as fixing an outage, is a stated use of Access Transparency.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Overview of Access Transparency”, “When to use Access Transparency”
notes.evidence: Verifying that Google personnel are accessing your content only for valid business reasons, such as fixing an outage or attending to your support requests.

notes.front: Does access to Compliance Reports Manager cost extra?
notes.back: No. It gives on-demand access to its compliance resources at no additional cost.
notes.explanation: Some resources need a sign-in with a Google Cloud or Google Workspace account.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Compliance reports manager”, “Compliance Reports Manager”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: An auditor asks a customer for Google Cloud's latest security certificates and audit reports. Where can the customer get them on demand?
notes.back: Compliance Reports Manager.
notes.choices:
A) Cloud Audit Logs
B) Access Transparency
C) Compliance Reports Manager
D) Security Command Center
